questions.stem: Petunia, 62, has had constant right forefoot pain for 3 weeks that eases when she hangs the leg down. In the ED you do Buerger's test: she lies flat while you raise both legs, then she sits up with her legs over the side of the trolley. Which finding shows severe ischaemia of the right leg?
options: Right foot stays pink at 90° and its veins refill within 10 seconds when hung down
Right foot goes pale below 20° of elevation, then turns dusky red when hung down
Right foot turns blue when raised, and the blue colour fades once it is hung down
Right foot goes pale only at 80°, and its colour returns within 10 seconds when hung down
questions.why: A Buerger's angle (the elevation at which the foot goes pale) below 20°, followed by dusky red reactive hyperaemia (dependent rubor) when the leg hangs down, means severe ischaemia. A well-perfused leg stays pink at 90°.
notes: This is a normal result: a well-perfused foot stays pink at full elevation and its veins refill quickly when it hangs down.
An ischaemic foot goes pale (not blue) when raised and turns red when it hangs down. Blue on raising that fades on hanging down is the reverse of the expected pattern.
Going pale only near 90° and recovering colour quickly is at most mild disease. It does not fit an ABI of 0.28 with rest pain.

questions.stem: Petunia, 62, is waiting in a rural ED for transfer to the tertiary vascular unit. Her right foot has dry black gangrene of the first three toes with a sharp line of demarcation, and no redness, pus or moist tissue. WCC is normal and CRP is 12. What is the most appropriate care of her foot while she waits?
options: Raise the right leg on pillows to reduce swelling and ease her pain
Start IV flucloxacillin to stop the dry gangrene from becoming wet
Keep the leg hanging down, apply a dry non-adherent dressing and offload the heel
Debride the black toes at the bedside so the tissue underneath can be assessed today
questions.why: In CLTI, letting the leg hang down helps the little perfusion she has. Dry gangrene should be kept dry and protected under a non-adherent dressing, with the heels offloaded to prevent pressure ulcers. Leave debridement to the vascular team.
notes: Raising the leg lowers perfusion pressure to an already critically ischaemic foot and makes her rest pain worse.
There is no clinical or laboratory sign of infection, so antibiotics are not indicated. The foot should be watched for any change to wet gangrene.
Debriding non-viable tissue in an unrevascularised foot can create a wound that will not heal. Decisions about debridement and amputation belong to the vascular team after they have imaged her.

questions.stem: Petunia, 62, has severe right leg arterial disease (ABI 0.28). She sleeps half sitting up with her right leg over the edge of the bed. Her forefoot pain gets worse within a minute of lying flat and eases when she hangs the leg down. What best explains this pattern?
options: Hanging the leg drains venous blood from the toes and lowers their tissue pressure
Lying flat triggers sympathetic vasoconstriction of her collateral arteries
Hanging the leg compresses sensory nerves and damps the ischaemic pain signals
Gravity adds hydrostatic pressure and raises perfusion pressure beyond the block
questions.why: Beyond a severe blockage, the arterial pressure reaching the foot is very low. When the leg hangs down, the weight of the column of blood (hydrostatic pressure) adds to that pressure and improves blood flow to the toes. When she lies flat she loses that help, and at night cardiac output also falls.
notes: Venous congestion builds up when the leg hangs down; it does not fall. A lower venous pressure is not why the ischaemic toes feel better.
Lying flat does not cause collateral arteries to clamp down. The vessels beyond the blockage are already maximally dilated, and the problem is a lack of driving pressure.
Hanging the leg does not compress any nerve. The relief comes from better perfusion, not from blocking pain signals.

questions.stem: The ED registrar is measuring Petunia's right ankle pressures with a handheld Doppler and has already found the dorsalis pedis signal. Petunia is 62 and has suspected chronic limb-threatening ischaemia. Where should the probe go next to find the posterior tibial artery?
options: On the top of the foot, just lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon
Behind the lateral malleolus, midway between it and the calcaneal tendon
In front of the medial malleolus, next to the tibialis anterior tendon
Behind the medial malleolus, midway between it and the calcaneal tendon
questions.why: The posterior tibial artery passes behind the medial malleolus in the tarsal tunnel, under the flexor retinaculum. It lies with the tibial nerve between the flexor digitorum longus and flexor hallucis longus tendons, about midway between the malleolus and the calcaneal tendon.
notes: This is where the dorsalis pedis artery is found, which has already been measured.
Behind the lateral malleolus lie the sural nerve and small saphenous vein. The posterior tibial artery does not run there.
The great saphenous vein runs in front of the medial malleolus. A venous signal there would give a misleading result.
